sa.prompt: Detail the metabolic and enzymatic adaptations that occur in pediatric skeletal muscle following structured anaerobic training.
sa.model: Following anaerobic training, children exhibit key metabolic and enzymatic enhancements: (1) Increased resting intramuscular concentrations of phosphocreatine (PCr), adenosine triphosphate (ATP), and glycogen; (2) Increased activity of phosphofructokinase (PFK), the rate-limiting enzyme of anaerobic glycolysis; (3) Higher maximal blood lactate concentrations following exhaustive exercise, reflecting enhanced glycolytic energy contribution; and (4) Higher ventilatory thresholds, allowing sustained higher relative work intensities.
criteria: List increased resting stores of PCr, ATP, and glycogen.
Identify increased activity of phosphofructokinase (PFK).
Mention higher maximal blood lactate concentrations and elevated ventilatory thresholds.

sa.prompt: Explain how adult training principles should be adapted when designing conditioning programs for children to optimize adaptations while minimizing physiological and psychological risks.
sa.model: Standard adult training principles—such as progressive overload, specificity, and adaptation—apply directly to youth program design. However, coaches must apply these principles conservatively. Progression must be carefully monitored to protect developing bones and growth plates from overuse injury. Furthermore, conservative loading prevents overtraining syndrome, chronic fatigue, and psychological burnout, ensuring long-term athletic development and sustained interest in sports.
criteria: State that standard adult training principles (overload, specificity) apply to youth.
Advocate for conservative progression to avoid overuse injury and growth plate strain.
Highlight the importance of preventing overtraining and psychological burnout/loss of interest in sports.
